a. **Apply Axis Movement:** Create a tentative position $P_{tentative}$ by adding only the current axis component of $\Delta$ to the current safe position $P_{safe}$ [S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial].

Both Source [S2] and Source [S3] describe an axis-separated collision detection method. [S2] explicitly states: 'Iterate through each axis... Calculate target_position by adding the delta component of the current axis to the new position... If collided is false, update camera.position[axis]'. This matches the claim's description of creating a tentative position by adding only the current axis component of the delta to the current position (or safe position, as the previous axis movements are committed). [S3] notes describe a similar process: 'Apply velocity on X axis... If any point intersects, reset X position to previous safe value... Repeat steps 1-3 for Z axis... Repeat steps 1-3 for Y axis'. This confirms the logic of applying movement axis by axis and reverting to a safe position if a collision occurs.

d. **Resolve:** If collision detected, discard the movement for this axis ($P_{safe}$ remains unchanged) [S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial].

The claim states that if a collision is detected, the movement for that specific axis is discarded (the position remains unchanged). Source [S2] explicitly describes an algorithm where movement is applied axis by axis; if a collision is detected for a specific axis, the code 'update[s] camera.position[axis]' only if 'collided' is false, effectively discarding the movement for that axis. Source [S3] notes also confirm this logic: 'If any point intersects, reset X position to previous safe value,' which is equivalent to discarding the movement for that axis. Both sources support the claim.
